title: The same self in every being
hook: on the steps at Varanasi, the great teacher Shankara tells a man to move aside, and the man's question stops him
carry: sama-darshana: one self in every being
tomorrow: Why does a yoga book begin with Shiva?

segments.voice: Yesterday, trataka came home with the tortoise: pratyahara, the senses drawn in, so the mind can rest on God.
screen: `TRATAKA.` · `PRATYAHARA: SENSES DRAWN IN LIKE THE TORTOISE.`

segments.voice: Varanasi, early morning, the stone steps down to the Ganga. The young teacher Shankara is walking down to bathe, his students around him. Coming up the narrow lane is a man his society treated as outcaste, a chandala, with four dogs at his heels. Shankara calls out the old command: move aside, keep your distance. The man doesn't move. He asks a question instead, and it stops the great teacher where he stands.
screen: `VARANASI, THE STEPS TO THE GANGA.` → `MOVE ASIDE, SAYS THE TEACHER.` → `THE MAN ASKS A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: In the telling handed down with a short poem credited to Shankara, the Manisha Panchakam, the man asks, in paraphrase: what do you want moved away from what? This body from that body, both made of food? Or the Self from the Self, which is the same in both? Shankara, the story goes, bows to him and says that whoever sees this way is his teacher, whatever their birth. Many tellers add that the man was Shiva himself. What Shankara is caught out on is the Gita's own teaching. In chapter six, Krishna describes the one whose mind has become steady in yoga. In paraphrase: such a person sees the Self, the atman, abiding in all beings, and all beings in the Self, and sees the same everywhere. The Sanskrit is sama-darshana: same-seeing. Then Krishna makes it personal: whoever sees me everywhere, and everything in me, I am not lost to them, and they are not lost to me. Two verses later he gives that evenness a heart. In paraphrase: the one who, by the measure of one's own self, sees pleasure or pain in every being as the same, that yogi is held to be the highest. Shankara's commentary reads it plainly: as pain is unwelcome to me, so it is to every being. So this week's steady gaze was never only about a candle. It trains the eyes to look at a stranger, a rival, someone who was rude, and see the same Self looking back. An even gaze isn't a cold one.
screen: `BODY FROM BODY, OR SELF FROM SELF?` · `SHANKARA BOWS.` · `THE SELF IN ALL, ALL IN THE SELF.` · `OTHERS' PAIN AS YOUR OWN.` · then, large: `ONE SELF IN EVERY BEING.`

segments.voice: Rest the gaze on one small point, a flame or a mark, for a little while, blinking when you need to. Then let the gaze soften and widen, without moving the eyes, until it takes in the whole room, and look at all of it with the same calm you gave the point. Bring to mind one person you find hard, and if you pray, greet the same Self in them silently; if not, simply wish them well.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Teachers read the Gita's even gaze as where that calm leads: resting on every being the same.
Your line: sama-darshana: one self in every being. Tomorrow, the hands. I'll be here tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Hindus speak of seeing God, or the one Self, in every being, and the story of Shankara and the chandala at Varanasi is often told alongside the Gita's sama-darshana to teach it.

fork.setup: you're Shankara on the steps at Varanasi. the man with the dogs asks if you want the Self moved away from the Self. what do you do?
options: repeat the order to move aside.
bow to him as your teacher.
fork.reveal: in the telling, Shankara bows and says whoever sees the one Self this way is his teacher, whatever their birth.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: sama-darshana, same-seeing, an even gaze. In the Gita, the one steady in yoga sees the same everywhere.

trapdoor: what you thought: an even gaze means treating everyone coolly.
what it means: seeing the same Self in every being, and feeling their pain as your own.
what a scholar hears: Gita 6.29, sarvatra sama-darśanaḥ, 6.32, ātmaupamyena, and the Manīṣā Pañcakam's annamayād annamayam.
recall: delighting in the good of all beings

chat.meaning: The Gita's steady one sees the same Self in all beings and feels their pain as their own. Shankara learned it from a man he'd told to move aside.
